item.content:encoded: Not to take either side on this, but we haven't exactly had the best record of being able to control invasive species. I think you underestimate just how good we are at controlling our environment; if a single non-anomalous plant species can threaten us with ecological disaster, it's no stretch to think that an anomalous entity might do even worse.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Most likely I'm stupid, but I fail to see how these things would "out-compete" us if we let them wander freely. The "competition" stage for apex life-form on Earth is essentially over and we've won. It's not just a matter of "they'll overwhelm us with sheer numbers!" it's a matter of we have the ways and means to dispose of huge numbers of these things long before they can even begin to appear to compete (particularly without opposable thumbs).

Not just referring to "competition with humans" but with virtually any higher-level being with the sufficient numbers to withstand them in the event of hostilities. It's just more likely to be humans because when an invasive species appears in one of our ecosystems, we hunt them down and root them out. And if it reaches a level where it would be ruining our food supply and/or wrecking ecosystems, that would gain it enough attention to warrant a massive effort on the part of humanity in wiping it out.

Odd thing/question/observation: would it still be considered natural/artificial selection if the things are evolving themselves? They're clearly determining what functions best for them, then assembling new pieces for themselves based on that determination. Would that make them more dangerous or less dangerous?

As in, would they be better at determining what's best for them rather than the process of evolution over generations via trial and error, or are their senses limited in the way human senses are, thus leading to "poor choices" that cause catastrophes? (Like, we think being able to fly would aid in our evolution, only to find out we're too big to fly properly, so we bulk up, only to find out we need much more energy just to maintain ourselves flying, leading to ecological disasters as we massively increase farmland/animal raising all at once?)

item.content:encoded:
I absolutely love the idea of this, as well as the execution, with the exception of the final paragraph. While describing the different "species" adds some really nice detail, it feels really clunky. Maybe a bit more variety in sentence structure would help. Of course, it could just be me being picky.

Regardless, upvoted for an excellent concept with sufficient development and near-perfect execution.

The one thing that is left unexplained is the exact process by which new components are manufactured. The only thing I can think of is by having them consume any scrap metal they encounter. Actually, having them consume any metal they encounter could be an interesting, although probably unnecessary, addition.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In theory, you could layer enough springs to get a few years' worth of power. The major problem is pressure on the regulator (from over-strong springs); distribution of pressure from multiple mainsprings is where the engineering-genius-from-hell would have to come in. The gearbox would have to weigh a hundred kilos or more.

One thing that I am vague on is the energy-transference system. Most of the way in, I am thinking it is purely kinetic: gear-driven spindles on the face of the clock of the like. But mention of remote-power connections and power control by the Collectors muddies the issue. Also, how does energy predation work?

Since these are capable of replacing lost instances through reproduction, are there any dissection/vivisection reports that could clarify their energy/'biology'? Is there some form of battery and energy conversion, or are they truly clockwork, somehow winding down another instance to wind up their spring?

Questions, questions. But definitely +1

item.content:encoded:
There is a conflict in the containment/description:

Under Containment - any containment breach will likely end without intervention, as SCP-816 requires access to SCP-816-1 in order to survive, and is not capable of moving SCP-816-1

Under Description - without SCP-816-1, SCP-816 would likely adapt to gain energy in a way that would allow it to expand beyond Site-P/██

One should be changed. Since they are dependent on it, I would suggest that the Containment be changed to have Agents periodically winding the Grandfather Clock to remove the possibility of a breach.

Even worse, it seems obvious to me that since the automata are capable of adapting to changing circumstances, if the clock were permitted to run down, they'd find an alternate source of energy. And most modern houses are just filled with electrical outlets. And if you cut off the power to the house, well, it is possible to extract energy from decaying corpses, like the researchers… and anyone else in that town…

Upvoted. One suggestion, however: I would recommend changing one line, to state that the design is "precise to a degree not previously thought to be humanly possible." Obviously, unless 343 made these things, their design was humanly possible. :)

item.content:encoded:
I like the concept, but nothing here really feels new. There's already an alien/unnatural ecosystem SCP-440 and SCP-217 covers the clockwork angle. I think this needs a rewrite to make it more unique from those two.

I want to know more about the ecosystem aspect. Most of this SCP sounds like it's just a robo-bug generator, but then you touch on a food-chain and stuff. That sounds like it could be very interesting, and would help round out concept, give it some depth. I don't really want a list of bugs, I want to know how the ecosystem functions as a whole, and why, if got loose, it would be a problem. How quickly do the herbivore machines eat, were these machines found in just one room, stuck in a loop of eating only themselves, or were they spreading slowly from the clock?

I'm not going to vote, because I don't dislike it, but it needs something more.
